latin.171: GAR. Quod si aliqua esset in voce peccati Adae, homonymia & ambiguitas, illa tamen omnino sublata est, cum imputatio primi peccati Adae nuncupatur. Ita enim unusquisque per se facile intelligere potest, cum plura fuerint Adami peccata, de uno illo quaeri, quod inter omnia primum fuit, & quo non aliud est in genere humano prius. Ubi enim de numero vel ordine agitur, primum illud dici omnes intelligunt, unde ducitur numeri ordinisque principium, & quo prius nihil est in illo ordine. Itaque non erat hic istis distinctionum argutiis distinguendus, id est obturbandus magis, quam instruendus Lector.
latin.172: PLAC. Parum abest quin credam, hanc primi peccati Adae distinctionem Viro Docto commovisse bilem: adeo eam omni ex parte adoritur & sollicitat. Quid autem probare instituit? illam non necessariam fuisse. Fac ita esse; modo non sit falsa, non sit absurda, non sit causae meae noxia, causam non video, cur tantopere debeat exagitari. At distinguit & obturbat Lectorem. Distinguit forte, sed non diu. Obturbat autem neminem, nisi si quis me damnatum velit & confutatum. Lux distinguit & recreat: tenebrae confundunt & turbant. Praeterea nego non fuisse necessariam illam distinctionem. Ita enim distinctis subjecto & attributo quaestionis irritus fit eorum labor, qui meam sententiam tanto molimine oppugnant: quae causa videtur esse, cur hae distinctiones eis tantopere ingratae fuerint. Sed, inquit, unusquisque per se facile intelligere potest, cum plura fuerint Adami peccata, de uno illo quaeri, quod inter omnia primum fuit. Ergo id expressi, quod quisque per se facile intelligere potest: Grande scilicet crimen, & quod magnam reprehensionem meretur!
latin.173: At, inquam, hoc non sufficit. Progredi longius oportet. Peccatum enim Adami inter omnia primum duo complectitur, peccatum actuale, & peccatum habituale: illud omnium peccatorum actualium, hoc omnium habitualium primum: illud transiit, hoc mansit, & in posteros propagatum est, & quin nobis proxime seu immediate, cum intra nos sit, imputetur, nemo non Pelagianus ambigit. De altero illo an imputetur immediate, omnis est inter nos excitata controversia. Haec distinctio, quia audienti nominari primum Adae peccatum non statim veniebat in mentem, multumque habebat ad decidendam quaestionem momenti, constituenda fuit ob oculos Lectoris.
latin.174: GAR. Sed & in hac subjecti distinctione nonnulla continentur, quae bene perpendenti vix est ut probari valeant. Nam 1. Quo fructu secunda peccati Adae significatio distinguitur a tertia, cum quicquid de peccato Adae in secunda significatione hic dicitur, ei reapse convenire asseratur, non quatenus est actio transiens, sed quatenus est corruptio habitualis & permanens? Ita enim peccatum Adae secundo & tertio modo dictum in idem revera coincidunt.
latin.175: PLAC. Magnas habeo Viro docto gratias non patienti quicquam a me dici absque fructu. Quanquam fructu, uti spero, non carebit haec distinctio suo tempore & loco. Coincidunt quidem secunda & tertia acceptio in eandem imputationem, sed differunt modo loquendi, & sunt eiusdem nominis acceptiones diversae. Distinguere autem nomen, non rem ipsam, volui. Si quis dicat, id quod verum est, peccatum Adae dividi posse in primum peccatum actuale, & primum peccatum habituale; dividendum erit peccatum Adae acceptum secundo modo: divisi primum membrum erit peccatum Adae sumptum primo modo, & secundum membrum erit peccatum Adae tertio modo. Quibus si addas propagatam in nos corruptionem, quae vetus Adam solet nuncupari, etiam peccatum Adae vocari posse, habebis omnes illas acceptiones quas enumeravi, nihil ut sit, quare tanto conatu rejiciantur.
latin.176:
GAR. 2. Quomodo ista componi possunt inter se? Peccatum Adae imputatur nobis, non qua haesit in ipso, & peccatum Adae imputatur nobis qua fuit vitiositas permanens in ipso: nam haerere in Adamo, & esse permanens in Adamo, quid hic differant, ego quidem non video.

PLAC. Propositio, Peccatum Adae imputatur nobis, non qua haesit in ipso, mea quidem est; sed illi opposita, Peccatum Adae imputatur nobis qua fuit vitiositas permanens in ipso, mea non est. Voces enim in ipso, quae contradictionem efficiunt, non invenit in meis scriptis, sed de suo Vir doctus addidit hoc loco: neque vero illae comparent in sententiae meae expositione quam ipse praemiserat § x. Contradictionem igitur istam ipse fecit ac finxit, mihique falso tribuit.
latin.177:
GAR. 3. Quando dicitur primi nostri parentis corruptio nobis posteris illius imputari, non quatenus haesit in ipso Adamo, sed quatenus transiit in nos: quanam est illa, quae statim profertur, hujus rei ratio; quod scilicet corruptio nostra haereditaria, sit ejusdem speciei cum corruptione, quae fuit in Adamo? An igitur specifica illa duarum corruptionum identitas id efficit, ut prior nobis imputetur? Quod si est, nihil causae dici potest, cur non omnium nostrorum majorum corruptio nobis imputari dicenda sit &c.

PLAC. Hic quoque monstrum sibi fingit, quod debellet. Meam enim istam rationem & truncat, & perperam interpretatur. Truncat: omittit enim & verba immediate praecedentia, ac ut verbis utar Calvini, quia intra nos est, & sequentia, ac quam suam naturam, tam suam corruptionem moralem nobiscum Adamus communicavit. Male interpretatur: Non enim verbis illis, Est enim corruptio nostra haereditaria eadem specie cum illa quae olim fuit in Adamo, rationem reddere volui, cur peccatum Adami tertio modo acceptum nobis imputetur; sed cur dicatur intra nos esse. Quare imputetur ostendi, cum dixi, ac ut verbis utar Calvini, quia intra nos est: id quod causalis quia monere eum potuisset, si voluisset attendere. Dixi ergo cum Calvino ad Rom. 5. 17. ideo imputari, quia intra nos est: Posse autem intra nos dici, quia corruptio nostra haereditaria est eadem specie cum illa quae fuit in Adamo. Idque illustravi similitudine ducta ab ipsa natura nostra, quae, quia specie eadem est cum natura Adami, & ab ea propagata, inde fit ut dici possit Adamus naturam suam nobiscum communicasse: non minus autem nobiscum communicavit corruptionem suam, seu peccatum. Potest igitur dici peccatum Adami in nos propagatum, in nos introiisse, intra nos esse. Haec est ratiocinii mei vis; a qua vides, Lector, quam aberret D. Garissolius.

pass_a.171: GAR. But if there were any homonymy and ambiguity in the word of Adam's sin, that nevertheless is wholly removed when the imputation of the first sin of Adam is named. For so each one by himself can easily understand, since there were many sins of Adam, that inquiry is made concerning that one which among all was first, and than which nothing else is prior in the human race. For where there is dealing about number or order, all understand that that is said first from which the principle of number and of order is drawn, and than which nothing is prior in that order. Therefore the Reader was not here to be distinguished by those subtleties of distinctions, that is, more to be disturbed than instructed.
pass_a.172: PLAC. I am not far from believing that this distinction of the first sin of Adam moved the bile of the Learned Man: so much does he attack and harass it from every side. But what does he set out to prove? that it was not necessary. Grant that it is so; provided it is not false, is not absurd, is not injurious to my cause, I do not see a cause why it ought to be so greatly agitated. But it distinguishes and disturbs the Reader. It distinguishes perhaps, but not for long. But it disturbs no one, unless if someone should wish me condemned and confuted. Light distinguishes and refreshes: darkness confounds and troubles. Moreover I deny that that distinction was not necessary. For so, the subject and attribute of the question having been distinguished, the labor of those who with so great effort oppose my opinion becomes vain: which seems to be the cause why these distinctions have been so greatly displeasing to them. But, he says, each one by himself can easily understand, since there were many sins of Adam, that inquiry is made concerning that one which among all was first. Therefore I expressed that which each by himself can easily understand: a great crime indeed, and one that deserves great rebuke!
pass_a.173: But, I say, this does not suffice. It is necessary to advance further. For the sin of Adam first among all embraces two things, actual sin, and habitual sin: that the first of all actual sins, this the first of all habitual: that passed, this remained, and was propagated into posterity, and that it is imputed to us proximately or immediately, since it is within us, no one who is not a Pelagian doubts. Concerning that other, whether it is imputed immediately, the whole controversy stirred among us exists. This distinction, because when the hearer heard the first sin of Adam named it did not at once come into mind, and it had much moment for deciding the question, had to be set before the eyes of the Reader.
pass_a.174: GAR. But also in this distinction of the subject some things are contained which to one weighing well it is scarcely possible that they can be approved. For 1. With what fruit is the second signification of Adam's sin distinguished from the third, when whatever is here said of Adam's sin in the second signification is asserted to agree with it in reality, not insofar as it is a transient action, but insofar as it is habitual and permanent corruption? For so Adam's sin said in the second and third mode coincide in the same thing in reality.
pass_a.175: PLAC. I have great thanks to the learned Man for not suffering anything to be said by me without fruit. Although this distinction, as I hope, will not lack its fruit in its time and place. The second and third acceptation indeed coincide in the same imputation, but they differ in the manner of speaking, and are diverse acceptations of the same name. But I wished to distinguish the name, not the thing itself. If anyone should say, what is true, that Adam's sin can be divided into the first actual sin, and the first habitual sin; Adam's sin accepted in the second mode will have to be divided: of the divided, the first member will be Adam's sin taken in the first mode, and the second member will be Adam's sin in the third mode. To which if you add the corruption propagated into us, which is wont to be named old Adam, and can also be called Adam's sin, you will have all those acceptations which I enumerated, so that there is nothing why they should be rejected with so great effort.
pass_a.176: GAR. 2. How can these things be composed among themselves? Adam's sin is imputed to us, not as it stuck in him, and Adam's sin is imputed to us as it was permanent viciousness in him: for to stick in Adam, and to be permanent in Adam, what they differ here, I indeed do not see. PLAC. The proposition, Adam's sin is imputed to us, not as it stuck in him, is indeed mine; but the opposite to it, Adam's sin is imputed to us as it was permanent viciousness in him, is not mine. For the words in him, which make the contradiction, he did not find in my writings, but the learned Man added from his own at this place: nor indeed do they appear in the exposition of my opinion which he himself had set forth beforehand in § x. Therefore that contradiction he himself made and invented, and falsely attributed to me.
pass_a.177: GAR. 3. When it is said that the corruption of our first parent is imputed to us his posterity, not insofar as it stuck in Adam himself, but insofar as it passed into us: what then is that reason of this matter which is at once brought forward; namely that our hereditary corruption is of the same species with the corruption which was in Adam? Does therefore that specific identity of the two corruptions effect this, that the prior is imputed to us? Which if it is so, nothing of a cause can be said why the corruption of all our ancestors should not be said to be imputed to us &c. PLAC. Here also he fashions for himself a monster which he may conquer. For that reason of mine he both truncates and wrongly interprets. He truncates: for he omits both the words immediately preceding, and that I may use Calvin's words, because it is within us, and the following, and that Adam communicated with us as his nature, so his moral corruption. He interprets badly: For I did not wish by those words, For our hereditary corruption is the same in species with that which once was in Adam, to give a reason why Adam's sin accepted in the third mode is imputed to us; but why it is said to be within us. Why it is imputed I showed when I said, and that I may use Calvin's words, because it is within us: which causal because could have warned him, if he had been willing to attend. I said therefore with Calvin on Rom. 5:17 that it is therefore imputed, because it is within us: But that it can be said to be within us, because our hereditary corruption is the same in species with that which was in Adam. And that I illustrated by a likeness drawn from our nature itself, which, because it is the same in species with Adam's nature, and propagated from it, thence it comes about that Adam can be said to have communicated his nature with us: but no less did he communicate with us his corruption, or sin. Therefore Adam's sin can be said to have been propagated into us, to have entered into us, to be within us. This is the force of my reasoning; from which you see, Reader, how far D. Garissoles wanders.

171: Garissoles: But if there were any homonymy or ambiguity in the word "Adam's sin," it is wholly removed once we name the imputation of Adam's first sin. Anyone can see for himself that, though Adam had many sins, the question concerns the one that was first among them—nothing earlier in the human race. Where number or order is in view, everyone understands by "first" that from which the series begins, and before which nothing stands in that order. So the reader did not need to be tangled in these subtleties of distinction—that is, more disturbed than taught.
172: Placeus: I am nearly sure this distinction of Adam's first sin stirred the learned man's bile: he attacks and worries it from every side. What does he mean to prove? That it was unnecessary. Grant that; so long as it is not false, not absurd, and not harmful to my cause, I see no reason why it should be so fiercely chased. "But it distinguishes and confuses the reader." It distinguishes, perhaps—but not for long. It confuses no one unless someone wants me condemned and refuted. Light distinguishes and refreshes; darkness confounds and unsettles. Besides, I deny that the distinction was unnecessary. Once subject and attribute of the question are distinguished, the labor of those who batter my view with such effort is wasted—which seems why these distinctions so greatly displeased them. "But," he says, "anyone can easily see for himself that, though Adam had many sins, the question concerns the one that was first among them." So I stated what anyone can easily see for himself: a grave crime indeed, and one that deserves sharp rebuke!
173: But that, I say, is not enough. We must go further. Adam's first sin among all embraces two things: actual sin and habitual sin—the first of all actual sins, and the first of all habitual ones. The former passed; the latter remained and was propagated to posterity; and that it is imputed to us proximately or immediately, since it is within us, no non-Pelagian doubts. About the other—whether it is imputed immediately—the whole controversy among us has been raised. Because that distinction did not leap to mind as soon as a hearer heard "Adam's first sin" named, and because it mattered much for deciding the question, it had to be set before the reader's eyes.
174: Garissoles: But in this distinction of the subject as well there are points that, well weighed, can scarcely be approved. For (1) what is gained by distinguishing the second sense of Adam's sin from the third, when whatever is said here of Adam's sin in the second sense is claimed to fit it in reality not as a passing act but as habitual, lasting corruption? So Adam's sin in the second and third modes really coincides in the same thing.
175: Placeus: I thank the learned man for allowing nothing I say to go without fruit. Still, I hope this distinction will not lack its fruit in due time and place. The second and third senses do coincide in the same imputation, but they differ in manner of speaking and are diverse senses of the same name. I meant to distinguish the name, not the thing itself. If one says—what is true—that Adam's sin can be divided into the first actual sin and the first habitual sin, then Adam's sin taken in the second sense must be divided: the first member of the division will be Adam's sin taken in the first sense, and the second member Adam's sin in the third. Add the corruption propagated into us, commonly called old Adam and able to be called Adam's sin as well, and you have all the senses I listed—so there is no reason to reject them with such zeal.
176: Garissoles: (2) How can these be reconciled? "Adam's sin is imputed to us not as it stuck in him," and "Adam's sin is imputed to us as it was lasting viciousness in him"—for what difference is there here between "sticking in Adam" and "being lasting in Adam"? I do not see. Placeus: The proposition "Adam's sin is imputed to us not as it stuck in him" is mine; the opposite, "Adam's sin is imputed to us as it was lasting viciousness in him," is not. The words "in him," which create the contradiction, he did not find in my writings; the learned man added them here from his own stock. Nor do they appear in the exposition of my view that he himself had set out earlier in §x. So he made and invented that contradiction and falsely pinned it on me.
177: Garissoles: (3) When our first parent's corruption is said to be imputed to us his posterity not as it stuck in Adam himself but as it passed into us, what is that reason instantly offered—namely that our hereditary corruption is of the same species as the corruption that was in Adam? Does that specific identity of the two corruptions make the former imputed to us? If so, nothing can explain why the corruption of all our ancestors should not likewise be said to be imputed to us, and so on. Placeus: Here too he invents a monster to slay. He both truncates my reason and misreads it. He truncates: he omits the words immediately before—and, to use Calvin's phrasing, "because it is within us"—and what follows: that Adam shared with us both his nature and his moral corruption. He misreads: by those words "For our hereditary corruption is the same in species as that which once was in Adam" I did not mean to explain why Adam's sin in the third sense is imputed to us, but why it is said to be within us. Why it is imputed I showed when I said, again with Calvin, "because it is within us"—a causal "because" that could have warned him had he cared to listen. So with Calvin on Romans 5:17 I said it is imputed because it is within us; and that it can be called within us because our hereditary corruption is the same in species as that which was in Adam. I illustrated that by a likeness from our very nature: since it is the same in species as Adam's and propagated from him, Adam can be said to have shared his nature with us—and no less his corruption, or sin. So Adam's sin can be said to have been propagated into us, to have entered us, to be within us. That is the force of my reasoning; from it, reader, you see how far Dr. Garissoles strays.
